evidence.label: Planar Graph Metrics Embed into L1 with Constant Distortion
L1 Embeddings of Graphs of Bounded Treewidth

headline: Every planar road network can be redrawn in taxicab distance with stretch below one fixed number.
scope: Finite connected networks with positive edge lengths that are planar, or whose tree decompositions have bags of bounded size.
plain: Distances along roads in a network can often be copied into taxicab distance, but usually with some stretch. These two papers prove that planar networks need only a bounded stretch, whatever their size or road lengths. Networks of bounded treewidth are close to trees in a precise sense. They need a stretch depending only on that closeness. This settles two cases of a conjecture published in 2004 by Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair (Lean proof listed).
doesNot: This does not prove the full Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture, and it gives no value for the planar constant.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair, conjecture and treewidth-two case
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the planar and bounded-treewidth cases of a long-open conjecture linking distances and network cuts.

explanation:
Picture two towns, A and B. Each has a 1 km road to the same three villages. Distances follow the roads. A village is 1 km from each town. The two towns are 2 km apart, through any village. Any two villages are also 2 km apart.

Now try to redraw this map on a city grid. On a grid you add up the blocks walked in each direction. This is taxicab distance. Mathematicians call it L1 distance, and they allow as many directions as needed. Some maps fit a grid perfectly. Four corners of a square block, 1 km per side, already sit on grid corners. The towns-and-villages map does not fit. A small computer calculation over all cuts settles the best drawing. Even the best grid drawing must stretch some distance by 4/3 relative to another. That factor is called the distortion. In the best drawing, each distance lies between its true value and 4/3 of it, after one overall rescaling.

Why this kind of grid? A taxicab distance is a sum of cuts. A cut splits the places into two sides. Each cut adds its weight to every pair it separates. For the square block, take one north–south cut and one east–west cut, each of weight 1. Neighbouring corners are split by one cut, so they sit 1 km apart. Opposite corners are split by both, so they sit 2 km apart. Cuts are also how bottlenecks in networks are measured. Picture pipes carrying several kinds of goods between different pairs of places at once. The tightest cut caps how much can flow. The real best flow can fall short of that cap. The ratio between the two is the flow–cut gap. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair showed that the worst gap on a network equals its worst taxicab distortion.

The towns-and-villages map is planar: it can be drawn on paper with no roads crossing. In a 2004 paper, those four authors stated a broad conjecture. Take any proper minor-closed family of networks. Such a family stays inside itself when roads are deleted or shrunk to a point. It also leaves some network out. They predicted one fixed distortion for the whole family. It must not grow with the number of places or depend on road lengths. Planar networks form one such family. Networks of bounded treewidth form another.

Treewidth measures how tree-like a network is. Cover the places with small overlapping groups, called bags, arranged like the branches of a tree. Every road must fit inside some bag. The bag size needed says how tree-like the network is. The towns-and-villages map has treewidth two, the simplest case past trees.

Before these papers, the best general bound for planar maps still grew with size. Rao gave a bound of order the square root of log n, for n places, in 1999. Constant bounds existed only for special shapes. Gupta and coauthors proved the treewidth-two case. The best distortion there is exactly 2. Chakrabarti, Jaffe, Lee and Vincent gave the upper bound. Lee and Raghavendra gave the matching lower bound. Lee and Sidiropoulos handled bounded pathwidth, a stricter, path-like cousin of treewidth. Their route through random trees cannot reach all bounded-treewidth networks.

The one obstacle was scale. A large map has distances of many sizes. Close pairs and far pairs need different cuts. Each new layer of cuts can stretch short roads a little more. Over many scales, those small losses could pile up without limit. The planar paper makes its local cut rules agree exactly where neighbouring regions meet. It also narrows down which pairs still need work at each scale. The treewidth paper changes its random cuts in pairs, so the cut pattern on each bag stays the same.

Together, the two papers prove these two cases of the conjecture. Grow the towns-and-villages map to millions of places, with wildly uneven roads. If no roads cross, a taxicab drawing exists with distortion below one universal number. The same holds, with a number depending only on bag size, for networks of bounded treewidth. The theorems state that these numbers exist. The treewidth paper says it gives no explicit estimate for its number. Through the earlier link, the flow–cut gap is also capped on these networks. The full conjecture stays open. The planar paper says the needed gluing of larger pieces is not established.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of both main theorems. One gives a single distortion bound for all finite connected planar networks with positive road lengths. The other gives a bound depending only on bag size, for networks with a tree decomposition. The flow–cut consequences and the other corollaries are outside that check. No specialists have published a review yet.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean formalizations of both main theorems are listed. The flow–cut and other corollaries are not machine-checked. No constants are given, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Distance found by adding up the differences in each coordinate separately, like walking city blocks.
The largest factor by which a redrawing stretches some distance relative to another, after one overall rescaling.
A split of a network's places into two sides; it separates every pair on opposite sides.
A network that can be drawn on paper with no two roads crossing.
A measure of how tree-like a network is, based on the size of overlapping groups arranged like a tree.
A family of networks that stays inside itself when roads are deleted or shrunk to a point.
How far the best possible multi-pair flow in a network can fall short of the limit set by its tightest cut.
